Terce
TURS
n. (the second little hour, said at the third hour of the day, about nine in the morning)
Latin tertia hora, the third hour; from tertius, third. Also written tierce.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Terce is the office of the third hour, about nine in the morning by the Jewish reckoning Scripture uses. Of all the little hours it has the strongest New Testament association, for the third hour is when the Spirit fell at Pentecost — Peter answered the charge of drunkenness by pointing to the clock, and the church has prayed at that hour in memory of it ever since. The hour's hymn in the Roman use is a prayer for the Spirit, which is a sound instinct rightly grounded. The third hour is also the hour of the crucifixion in Mark's reckoning. Scripture itself, however, attaches no obligation to the hour, and the honest Protestant judgment on terce is twofold. The commemorative instinct is good: a church that remembers Pentecost daily is not thereby superstitious, and “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud” (Psa 55:17) shows the Psalmist dividing his day much the same way. The error was to make the commemoration a required work, and to let a recited Latin office stand in for the thing commemorated. The Spirit is sought by asking, not by keeping an anniversary.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives tierce as a third, and in liturgical use the third of the lesser hours; third as the ordinal of three; and defines hour as the twenty-fourth part of the natural day, with Pentecost as the feast of the fiftieth day.

expand to see more

TIERCE, n. A third; the third of something. In the Romish breviary, one of the lesser hours of the office, said at the third hour of the day.

THIRD, a. The first after the second; the ordinal of three.

HOUR, n. A space of time equal to the twenty fourth part of the natural day.

PENTECOST, n. A solemn festival of the Jews, so called because celebrated on the fiftieth day after the sixteenth of Nisan; also, Whitsuntide, a festival of the christian church.

SPIRIT, n. In a theological sense, the Holy Spirit, the third person in the Trinity; also, an inspired or influencing power.

Key Scripture

Psa 55:17 — "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice."

Act 3:1 — "Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour."

Luk 18:1 — "And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;"

Act 10:9 — "On the morrow, as they went on their journey, and drew nigh unto the city, Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour:"

Modern Corruption

The third-hour office, kept in memory of Pentecost: a good commemoration turned into an owed recitation, and the Spirit sought by anniversary rather than by asking.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that remembering what God did at an hour is wholesome, while crediting the remembrance as a work is not. The hour itself commends nothing; the asking does: “men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luk 18:1).

Terce also shows the real cost of an office said in a language the sayer does not command. An hour appointed to seek the Spirit, recited by rote in Latin by a brother who could not construe it, is the exact case Paul reasons about when he insists that the understanding must be engaged in prayer and praise. The Reformers' demand for the vernacular was not a concession to taste; it was the recovery of a hour's whole purpose.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin tertius, third; Greek hora (G5610), an hour; Greek pneuma (G4151), spirit; Greek pentekoste (G4005), the fiftieth; Hebrew shalosh (H7969), three.

expand to see more

Latin tertius — third; the hour named for its place in the day.

Greek hora (G5610) — an hour; “to pray about the sixth hour” (Act 10:9) shows the same reckoning one hour on.

Greek pneuma (G4151) — spirit, breath, wind; the Person the hour's hymn addresses.

Greek pentekoste (G4005) — the fiftieth, the feast at whose third hour the Spirit was poured out.

Hebrew shalosh (H7969) — three; behind the Psalmist's threefold day of prayer.

Usage

"“Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray” (Psa 55:17) — the threefold division the little hours elaborate."

"“the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour” (Act 3:1) — apostolic practice marking hours without binding them."

"“men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luk 18:1) — the standing duty no hour discharges."
